paras: The stoning of Black railroad workmen at Lynchburg was an attack in 1882, some time before April 4, in which a party of young men threw stones at "the colored workmen" on the Richmond and Alleghany railroad at Lynchburg, Virginia. Several of the attackers were fined by the Mayor, while a Black worker who broke one attacker's collar-bone was sent on to the grand jury.

The only known account comes from the Lynchburg correspondent of the Richmond Dispatch, whose column, signed "Beaumont," was dated on April 4, 1882. The correspondent reported that "a party of dissipated young men" had been charged with attacking the colored workmen on the railroad with stones, without giving the date or place of the attack or naming anyone involved. In what the correspondent called an "affray" one of the young men had his collar-bone broken by one of the Black workers. No injury to any of the workmen is mentioned.

On the morning of April 4 the young men appeared before the Mayor, and several of them were fined. The Black worker who had broken the attacker's collar-bone was "sent on for indictment by the grand jury," a more serious step than the fines imposed on the attackers. No report of the grand jury's action on his case appears in the coverage.

The Dispatch ran the item as a three-sentence paragraph under the subhead "FRACAS" in a column of Lynchburg news that also covered small-pox in Bedford County, a railroad accident and local deaths. The report itself was flat in tone, calling the attackers "dissipated" and the workmen "colored" and "negroes," but the same column complained at length about the new postmaster's appointment of Black delivery clerks, calling one a "son of Ham." No other newspaper report of the attack was found.
